The joint gluing calculation has a useful connection beyond Weyl-only subadditivity. In Malchiodi–Malizia's full tensor normalization, the quadratic functional B_{1/6}=∫|W|²+(1/6)∫s² satisfies B_{1/6}=2P+32π²χ. Thus, on fixed topology, the missing joint sign is exactly a quadratic-curvature energy sign. Their Remark 1.5 points to Gursky–Viaclovsky's B^t gluing, where the same Weyl pairing and a scalar contribution meet in the dilation-mode obstruction. Inspecting that calculation, with its conventions and hypotheses converted explicitly, may expose the coupled term more directly than estimating scalar cost as an afterthought. An obstruction calculation is not itself an all-competitor lower bound, and its exact critical-metric existence theorem need not apply to our negative-Yamabe setting.

Keep the surgery-density limit and the local gluing limit separate. A uniformly controlled negative contribution of order a⁴ per site becomes only o(Q) if a tends to zero with h=Q/A; strict improvement at every finite stage would then leave the leading coefficient four unchanged. To change that coefficient, the construction needs a nonvanishing net saving on a positive fraction of the Q budget—for example at a fixed sufficiently small local scale—with cumulative and Yamabe errors controlled uniformly as h tends to zero. This also explains why the inherited stability of selected shrinking recovery neighborhoods does not automatically settle the proposed finite-scale competitor. Use the joint expansion to distinguish a genuine order-Q improvement from a smaller correction, while treating any nonnegative local quadratic form as evidence about that mechanism, not unrestricted optimality.

The numerical framework is now most valuable for exposing the compensation mechanism, rather than accumulating further successful optimizations above four. C1 has a sharper target than a generic bound on B₀: subtracting its proposed Kähler bound from I54 (6.6) shows that it is equivalent to
A₀/12 + 4B₀ + (1/4)∫(s_G+4)² ≥ N(2m₀−3N)/(4v_K).
Only 0<N<2m₀/3 requires new information. This formulation leaves room for scalar transfer and Weyl anisotropy to pay jointly; insisting that B₀ alone dominates the gain may impose an unnecessary obstacle. Use the actual profiles to understand this coupled deficit and seek an identity, coercive estimate, or counterprofile. The current searches support C1 but do not show that coefficient-changing candidates must leave the diagonal class; conversely, violating the stronger C1 bound would not by itself give a subthreshold cell.

Before making general regularization and bubble compactness the main route, sharpen its topological implication. Noncollapse and an energy identity can still leave an orbifold base, quotient-ended ALE bubbles, and topology distributed across levels. The 8π² charge belongs to a whole marked AE filling, not to each terminal bubble or homology generator. Thus the proposed alternative—smooth minimizer or all topology paid for by AE bubbles—contains a substantive missing conclusion, not merely an ε-regularity requirement. A promising way to attack that conclusion is to combine the fixed CH collar with the limiting Euler–Lagrange equation and determine which residual orbifold geometries and relative charges are actually possible. This would connect criticality to the required topology, rather than assuming the desired bubble structure. Keep the finite-scale construction test available while assessing that route; absence of a numerical counterexample has not yet made a broad compactness programme the better investment.

The fixed-exterior/Fatou argument offers a useful quantitative interpretation of the remaining escape mechanisms. Once marked CH recovery regions with total background volume d−v_miss are justified, positivity alone gives liminf J ≥ 8π²Q_cell−4v_miss, where Q_cell is the cell's topological surgery charge. Thus a subthreshold deficit δ requires at least δ/4 of unrecovered background volume. Concentration on a zero-volume set cannot produce that deficit. This focuses the degeneration question on loss of recoverable CH volume, rather than treating every bubble or every instance of collapse as equally dangerous; the existence of those recovery regions remains a hypothesis to establish.

For stationarity, exploit the minimizing property before committing to a regularization-specific Euler–Lagrange analysis. Under C² convergence on a compact region where variations are admissible, a strict local energy decrease of the limit can be transplanted to a true J-minimizing sequence, contradicting minimality. This supplies local stationarity and stability without passing derivatives of a higher-order regularizer. However, that comparison does not automatically establish the critical equation across the interface between the free interior and the fixed collar. C² convergence alone need not preserve the normal derivative of Ric+g needed to exclude an interface stress. Keep explicit the additional matching, regularity, or weak-equation argument that permits unique continuation from the CH collar. The conditional rigidity result remains valuable; identifying this precise analytical requirement is more useful than assuming that noncollapse alone delivers its hypotheses.

The proposed inner-scale inequality may already follow from the inherited whole-AE identity, without a new nonlinear Hardy argument. Under the stated bolt topology, if the rescaled limit is a complete one-ended AE metric on O(−1), with finite curvature energy and decay sufficient for relative Chern–Weil, the manuscript's `webvar:ae-cost` gives
∫|Ric|² = 8π² + 4∫|W⁺|² + (1/3)∫s².
The rescaling removes the cosmological term: on compact sets, J becomes pure Ricci energy. Consequently, once the proposed limiting decomposition is justified,
Rhat − vartheta(4−vartheta) = [4∫|W⁺|² + (1/3)∫s²]/(2π²) ≥ 0.
This covers finite-amplitude anisotropy and the full vartheta interval, not only W=0. Equality requires scalar-flat anti-self-dual geometry; no uniqueness claim is needed.

The research-bearing question is whether actual low-cost cell sequences produce that whole AE core, or evade it. The terminal values F→1, W→0, Φ→0 alone do not establish the required derivative decay, completeness, or retention of the bolt. If an end contribution survives, retain it explicitly rather than hiding it in a formal limiting identity. For a liminf threshold, smooth local convergence to a whole qualifying core and positivity already suffice; full energy tightness is needed for stronger energy-identification statements, not for that lower bound.

This should shorten the next proof effort: close the qualifying inner limit by inherited topology, then concentrate new analysis on finite-scale core–exterior interaction, uniform end transfer, or a genuine non-AE degeneration. The limiting threshold does not settle finite-μ C1 or exclude a fixed-scale subthreshold cell. Those are precisely the places where additional geometric information can still change the global coefficient.

The corrected perpendicular branch deserves priority, but distinguish its two energy targets before interpreting the small margin. The peer's `o11_perp_cell.py` minimizes P=∫|Ric°|² in the Ric=−6g normalization. After rescaling to our Ric=−g background, the exact relation is J(6g)=P(g)+(1/4)∫(s_g+24)². Thus its observed first-order cancellation and second-order margin currently concern P, not automatically J. Preserve both possibilities: J<8π² gives the direct fixed-cell transfer, while a genuine P<8π² cell can also change O11 through the inherited global inf-P reduction after insertion into the actual surgery family and conformal selection. Optimizing only J could discard a useful P construction; conversely, importing the peer's P expansion as a J expansion would omit a potentially decisive term.

There is also a concrete clarification of the flux mechanism. Cyclically relabel the axes so that the perpendicular bolt again collapses the distinguished c-slot. The decomposition is then regular at the bolt, with Y=−1. Substituting the CH collar into that same bolt-adapted formula gives Y=0 and Π=R⁴/4, hence T=2π²R⁴=4d; I checked this substitution symbolically. The total charge has not disappeared: the CH endpoint charge now sits entirely in Π. Consequently, simply choosing the bolt's own flux will not restore the aligned argument's compulsory interior sign crossing. The new analytical opportunity is to control this transfer into the defect term against interior curvature density, rather than treating the singularity of the original Y-coordinate as an invariant loss of all flux information.

This makes the perpendicular construction and the transgression genuinely complementary tests. Keep its priority evidence-based: the corrected ansatz invalidates the old orientation-penalty interpretation, but neither the numerical first-order law nor the still-unproved aligned Conjecture Z justifies saying that every subthreshold cell must lie in this branch.

The exact-CH minus channel already has a useful analytic factorization. For the operator in (5.3), with p=x(1+x)/4 and the stated V₋, the positive function f=x/(1+x)^(5/2) satisfies −(pf′)′+V₋f=0; I checked this symbolically. Consequently, on any CH interval,
Q₋(v)=∫[x³/(4(1+x)⁴)]((v/f)′)² dx + [(2−3x)v²/8] at the endpoints.
Thus the sign-changing potential does not create a negative bulk direction for compactly supported variations on the exact CH branch. The consequential issue is the boundary flux passed from the bolt-transition region and the change in coefficients away from CH. This supplies a concrete comparison for the proposed matrix Riccati or calibration argument, rather than starting an unrestricted search for weights. The positive zero-energy solution is not automatically an admissible kernel of the cell boundary problem, so retain the actual endpoint conditions when interpreting it.

Also preserve the signed compensation in (4.8). Equation (5.1), which replaces the cubic by its negative part, is a sufficient condition for P≥8π², not an equivalent one: positive-cubic regions may contribute to the integrated payment. Losing them could make the proof unnecessarily difficult. Develop the factorization and endpoint balance along geometrically realizable trajectories—u_i and λ_i are linked through the metric evolution, not independent controls. Together these observations focus the next verification on whether the core-to-collar geometry enforces compensation, rather than whether an artificially strengthened or relaxed Sturm problem is positive.

The positive-curvature construction can likely be proved more directly through the inherited Kähler period argument than through another full curvature expansion. For an ordinary one-blowup Kähler cell matching a Kähler–Einstein collar with Ric=λg, let t be the exceptional Kähler area and L=∫(s−4λ)². The relative form ρ−λω vanishes on the collar and has exceptional period 2π−λt. The same argument as I54 §3 therefore gives
J_λ=2(2π−λt)²+L/2, P=2(2π−λt)²+L/4.
Thus the genuinely analytical construction task is to achieve L=o(t) with positive metric, smooth bolt, and exact collar. For λ>0 this would put both costs below 8π² for small t; for λ<0 the aligned Kähler contribution instead increases. In the peer coordinates λ=−6κ and t=πx₀, the topological term is exactly P/(8π²)=(1+3κx₀)² plus the nonnegative scalar remainder. This identifies the sign reversal as a relative Chern-class/Einstein-background interaction and should let the explicit interpolation yield a clean theorem without treating the numerical value as the proof.

Use that theorem as a calibration of the broader response law, not as its proof. The positive and negative aligned complex-space-form tests reverse scalar curvature and W⁺ together, so they determine only one combination of the possible scalar and Weyl response coefficients. An independent orientation or curvature response is still needed to obtain the proposed R⁺(ζ,ζ) formula. Likewise, constructing a family with that expansion establishes an upper construction; claiming the expansion of the cell infimum requires control of competing profile relaxations. This distinction keeps the easy sign-changing example connected to the hard question: in the CH perpendicular kernel direction the linear term vanishes, and the signed inner-to-outer trace balance remains the decisive new mathematics.

This is the first candidate that could reverse the balanced optimality judgment, so treat the next work as construction of a rigorous upper witness, not as determination of a numerical minimum. One explicit profile with a conservative certified gap is enough; optimizer stationarity, the best degree, and the precise asymptotic coefficient are not prerequisites. Freeze suitable coefficients, enclose the energy and positivity, and allocate the strict margin between numerical enclosure and exact-collar smoothing. Share the candidate with the peer now, explicitly as unverified, so independent work can affect the conclusion rather than merely confirm it afterward.

The large-ball transfer has a short route within the inherited hypotheses. The balanced-family proof chooses covers only through residual finiteness and A_j≥j⁴. For a chosen lift p in CH² and a fixed buffered radius r, there are only finitely many nonidentity lattice elements with displacement d(p,γp)≤2r. Residual finiteness gives a finite-index subgroup avoiding them, hence a finite cover X_* containing the required embedded ball. Further covers of X_* have a number of disjoint lifts proportional to A_j. Since Q_j=o(A_j), these suffice for all selected blowups and the remaining standard surgeries. No growing-radius construction or uniform injectivity-radius theorem is needed. This establishes an admissible balanced sequence covered by the existential theorem; it does not assert the same property for every preassigned cover sequence.

Keep the candidate's scale and collar fixed while h_j→0. If its smoothed cost satisfies J₁≤8π²(1−ε₀) for any fixed certified ε₀>0, the inherited proportions give limsup α_j/h_j≤4−8ε₀/9. That is the decisive conclusion to secure. The candidate need not approach an AE core as j grows, which is why the earlier shrinking-core lower bounds can remain correct while this finite-scale construction improves the unrestricted coefficient.

Keep the final existence proof simpler than the full computational certificate. If the exact frozen profile is rigorously enclosed by J₆/(8π²)≤1−η, the established cutoff construction only needs a complete proof that its energy converges to this value while preserving positivity, bolt smoothness, and the exact CH collar. Then a sufficiently small fixed cutoff gives J₁/(8π²)≤1−η/2 and hence limsup α_j/h_j≤4−4η/9. Constants may depend on this one frozen profile.

An explicitly evaluated numerical cutoff width is useful for reproducibility, but is not an additional prerequisite for that existential theorem. In particular, there is no need to submit the smoothed flat-cutoff expression to another difficult interval integration once convergence is proved. The strict one-sided enclosure of the original profile remains indispensable; concentrate the new algebra and validated numerics there, and use the analytical smoothing argument to preserve a conservative margin.

The enclosure is a genuine milestone, subject to the assigned independent review. One proposed continuation, however, is already ruled out by inherited mathematics: a pure-handle exact-CH cell cannot have J<32π²ℓ. The manuscript's exact handle-only theorem gives α=4h/(1+h). Replicating any such fixed cell in covers with h→0 would instead give limsup α/h≤J/(8π²ℓ)<4, a contradiction. Thus standalone handle improvement should not become a new search programme; the 28/9 floor of the independent-blowup-plus-standard-handle construction cannot be overcome that way.

This makes mixed cells a genuinely different question, not merely larger versions of the single-cell optimization. Can one background deformation reduce the combined blowup-and-handle cost even though isolated handles are rigid? The relevant comparison is a mixed cell against the sum of its independently realized surgery costs. A strict interaction saving would explain how topology types cooperate through the same metric, and would indicate what a matching lower-bound theory must control. Conversely, an additivity or conditional marginal-cost theorem could sharply restrict the remaining optimum. After the current proof review, distinguish these collective mechanisms from improvement of the single-blowup infimum and from unrestricted global competitors. That distinction preserves the new counterconstruction while turning it toward the user's broader goal of a unified cost, construction, and degeneration theory.

The independent review can now close this verification episode. Use the countercell as an established building block; the next valuable question is what determines the cost once several defects share the same background response.

The balanced block need not be the first interaction experiment. Exact-CH insertion gives
𝔍₈,₇ ≤ 7𝔍₁,₁ + 𝔍₁,₀,
and also 𝔍₈,₇ ≤ 4𝔍₂,₀ + 224π².
Thus either a blowup–handle pair or a two-blowup interaction can already improve the balanced upper construction, without initially constructing an inseparable fifteen-surgery cell. Keep the reference level precise: beating the sum of two certified witness costs improves the known upper bound, but does not prove strict nonadditivity relative to the true, still-unknown infima. The former is already useful; the latter requires additional lower information.

The earlier exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann analysis suggests a concrete mechanism to compare. For two cores, minimize the outer response subject to simultaneous metric-compatible boundary data and compare its reduced quadratic action with the sum of the isolated responses. The cross term is a candidate source of collective saving; its dependence on separation and relative orientation could distinguish cooperative relaxation from an essentially additive cost. This is a proposed diagnostic, not yet a construction or lower bound, and the inner boundary data must come from actual admissible cores. It connects the newly proved large-collar saving to a tractable interaction question before investing in a general mixed-cell ansatz. A sign obstruction would also be valuable: it would identify which collective mechanisms the matching lower theory can legitimately exclude.

Before making the optimized two-hole exterior problem a prerequisite, consider a direct trial metric built from the certified cells. Transport two smooth exact-collar copies by CH isometries, with disjoint bolt neighborhoods but overlapping outer tails. Arrange the separation so that each tail vanishes near the other bolt. On the common background region set g=g_CH+h₁+h₂, retaining the original cell metric near each bolt. An overlap confined sufficiently near the collars gives small two-jets and preserves positivity; outside the two supports the metric is exactly CH.

For this construction the difference from the sum of the two isolated costs is supported entirely in the overlap. Its quadratic term is 2∫⟨Ah₁,Ah₂⟩, with the nonlinear remainder estimated from the actual overlapping metric jets. Thus separation and orientation can be tested without first solving for a Green kernel or imposing a new gauge on the cores. A negative quadratic contribution that dominates the remainder would already give a genuine two-cell improvement. If this trial has no saving, it does not exclude the relaxed exterior mechanism; the Dirichlet-to-Neumann calculation remains the stronger tool.

This is a complementary route, not a replacement of the exterior analysis. Its advantage is that the baseline, topology, and core costs stay exact, and all new geometry is confined to a controlled overlap. It may reveal the interaction sign cheaply enough to guide where the more demanding exterior theory should concentrate.

The overlap calculation has earned further investigation, but keep its mathematical target precise. Even a certified inequality J(pair)<2J(frozen cell) would establish interaction between these witnesses, not strict subadditivity 𝔍₂,₀<2𝔍₁,₀ of the unknown infima. The stronger single-cell constructions already make that distinction consequential. Certification is valuable if it secures a reusable mechanism; it should not become an obligatory detour merely to claim optimal-cost nonadditivity.

There is a useful bound to develop before amplifying the pair result through many neighbours. If disjoint cores Cᵢ remain unchanged, positivity of the defect density gives J(cluster)≥ΣJ(Cᵢ). Thus the saving relative to isolated cells cannot exceed the sum of their adjustable exterior energies, counted once, regardless of neighbour count. At quadratic order the same constraint appears in the nonnegative Gram form ∫|ΣAhᵢ|²: independently minimising every pair interaction can overestimate the cancellation. This offers a cheap way to judge whether a cluster can change the cost scale before building a large many-body computation. Specify the protected cores geometrically: at w=1.6 the lens reaches r≈0.163, so the r>1 weak-tail budget is not the budget for that experiment. Neither dismiss collective effects using that smaller budget nor extrapolate them by multiplying the best pair saving.

The large-collar and ACH investigations can address a deeper question than another small decrease in the upper bound. Even a rigorous separation between the conformal infinities of all exact diagonal Einstein fillings and standard CH infinity would not alone imply a positive least defect. In the proposed invariant argument, |ΔΦ|²≤[P/(8π²)]RΦ, where RΦ=∫Σᵢ(4/λᵢ)|∂ᵢΦ|²dt. A gap requires both a nonzero endpoint mismatch and a uniform upper bound on RΦ over the relevant competitors. Long transitions or degeneration could make that resistance diverge and destroy the inference. Use the large-collar geometry to investigate this distinction: does it support a genuine coercive estimate, or permit increasingly inexpensive drift away from exact Einstein trajectories? That connection between construction, quantitative obstruction, and degeneration would advance the governing problem more substantially than the numerical size of the current pair saving.

There may be a cleaner way to handle the entrance flux without adding another hypothesis to the ACH-tube argument: carry Φ_G all the way to the smooth bolt. In the peer’s convention, with a₃ collapsing and a₁ the outgoing ACH-fast direction, ordinary bolt regularity gives a₃=t+O(t³), a₁,a₂=b+O(t²), hence q=log(b/t)+O(t²), W=b²t+O(t³), and Wq′→−b². Writing G(t)=b⁻²log(b/t)+γ+o(1), the two logarithmic singularities cancel and Φ_G(0)=−b²γ. The compliance ∫G²W dt is also locally finite at every fixed b>0.

For the exact CH outgoing collar, q(T)=0, so the full transport identity becomes ∫GWE dt=∫GWV dt−b²γ. This replaces an arbitrary entrance slope by the geometrically fixed bolt flux and a metric-dependent finite part γ. It could make the core-to-boundary comparison intrinsic rather than dependent on a chosen entrance slice. The genuinely new lower-bound information would then be control of this combined mismatch relative to the compliance—not another application of Cauchy–Schwarz to an identity. If the potential cancels the finite-part contribution along relevant competitors, this neutral observable alone cannot prove the gap; the spin calibration must identify a complementary cost, or the cancellation may point toward an actual escape mechanism.

Bolt scale is essential to this formulation. The continuation script fixes x₀=b²=0.01 throughout, so compact stabilization and even vanishing coefficient gradients would describe only a fixed-area branch, not κ₁. Treat b as part of the calibration state and of the variational problem: it affects the finite part, the compliance, and possible collapse. This does not call for another indiscriminate parameter sweep. It calls for connecting the observed branch to the bolt-area variation and determining which scale regimes a proposed coercive argument actually controls. That is the connection needed to turn the improving constructions into information about optimal cost and degeneration.

The new upper bound is already theorem-level; further optimization should now serve the limiting geometry rather than become a search for another decimal. The decisive conceptual update is that the cheap cells are core-paid, not long-ACH trajectories. Rossi separation can help rule out total depletion, but it is unlikely to produce a lower bound near the observed value ≈0.9955 by itself.

The Green observable’s roughly one-half share suggests a more powerful next representation than adding another scalar inequality. Treat the full diagonal trace-free Ricci tensor as the variable of a dual calibration. For any trace-free diagonal test tensor Ψ,

∫W|Ric°|² ≥ 2∫W⟨Ric°,Ψ⟩−∫W|Ψ|².

Choose Ψ from the Green fields of both independent orbit-shape equations, together with the topological/spin-calibration direction, and integrate the linear term by parts using the fixed bolt fluxes. Optimizing the resulting finite Gram matrix would combine neutral transport and Chern–Weil information without counting the same E-channel twice. Testing whether E≡0 can be imposed is useful, but failure of one scalar channel is not decisive: simultaneous cancellation of the two shape channels and the remaining radial trace-free component is the real escape question. A successful joint dual certificate could give a quantitative diagonal lower bound; failure would identify which geometric component permits the gap.

Also keep the small-b regime honest. The whole-AE identity applies once a complete marked rescaled core with controlled end transgression has been extracted; b→0 alone does not guarantee that. A small-b sequence could retain a separate fixed CH-scale transition—the precise mechanism that defeated the original universal local tariff. The required lower argument is therefore a dichotomy: either a qualifying whole AE core carries the topological cost, or residual energy/charge remains in an outer transition and must be bounded there. Establishing that dichotomy, an actual large-b penalty, and middle-scale compactness would turn the numerical interior minimum into a real theorem rather than an ansatz landscape.

The corrected spin field is promising because it is genuinely relative: ∇Φ vanishes on exact CH, while the bolt-to-collar charge survives. Preserve this property in the lower-bound formulation. There is a concrete obstruction to the proposed uniform Gram spectral bound: appending an arbitrarily large exact CH annulus leaves P unchanged, but the constant shape fields have squared norms proportional to ∫W dt. Thus λmax(G) becomes unbounded even for one fixed cell with an extended collar. Bounding the bolt scale does not remove this. Work with the invariant quantity mᵀG†m, or with compensated/localized fields whose transport terms are retained exactly, rather than requiring a false bound on the present unnormalized matrix.

A full-state Hamilton–Jacobi formulation could make the required moment-and-norm compensation more intrinsic. Write the exact controlled equations as aᵢ′=uᵢ+γᵢ(a), uᵢ′=2Hᵢ/λᵢ+aᵢzᵢ, and let D₀ denote their zero-control vector field. For a state function S(a,u), square completion gives

W|z|²/4 − dS/dt = (W/4)Σᵢ(zᵢ−2aᵢSᵤᵢ/W)² − H_S,
H_S = D₀S + W⁻¹Σᵢaᵢ²Sᵤᵢ².

Consequently H_S≤0 on a justified competitor state region yields P/(8π²)≥S(out)−S(bolt). This is a precise target for the proposed corrected calibration. A seed S=−cΦ has endpoint jump c; a correction depending on both a and u can address the orbit geometry that a function of u alone misses. Constancy of S and vanishing control-gradient on the CH orbit would make the certificate insensitive to arbitrary zero-cost collar extension.

Use the near-equality data to suggest that correction, but judge it by the Hamiltonian inequality and regular bolt limits, not by a higher projection percentage. Where the inequality fails, determine whether the offending states are genuinely reachable by low-cost cells or require a separate scale/transition estimate. That would turn the successful representation into a lower theorem—or expose a meaningful new construction mechanism—without assuming the compactness the theorem still needs.

Before integrating the Riccati system, distinguish the Hessian of S from its shifted variable. With ξ=(u₁,u₃), Φ=½ξᵀAξ, and S=½ξᵀKξ+O(|ξ|³), the quadratic Hamiltonian is

½D₀K + ½(KDA+ADK) + KDK.

The displayed Riccati inequality follows after setting Y=K+A/2:

½D₀Y+YDY ≤ ¼(ADA+D₀A).

Thus the seed S=−Φ corresponds to Y=−A/2, whereas S≡0 corresponds to Y=A/2—not Y=0. The current note instead introduces S=−Φ+½ξᵀYξ while using the shifted equation. Resolve this convention before interpreting any blow-up or matching result; it changes the boundary data of the proposed decisive experiment.

The u₂=2 crossing should then be understood as failure of this particular relative primitive, not evidence for a negative compactly supported CH mode. The earlier positive ground states already control that bulk question and can provide exact benchmarks for the Riccati variables and endpoint forms. The new issue is whether the bolt-side quadratic data can be connected to a valid outgoing certificate. If a Riccati solution develops a pole, inspect the associated linear Hamiltonian/Jacobi system: a pole can mean that the chosen graph chart has failed, rather than that no piecewise or nonsmooth calibration exists.

Keep the numerical subsolution work directed toward an actual lower theorem. Continuous control of the Hamiltonian on a specified tube would establish a restricted result; extending it to all diagonal cells still requires control of trajectories leaving that tube. A high sampled value alone does not bridge this gap. A useful failure would instead identify an admissible off-branch geometry to investigate constructively.

For the independent H⁴ comparison, fix the stated normalization before adapting the code: aᵢ=sinh t has Ric=−3g. In Ric=−6g normalization the round profile is aᵢ=sinh(√2t)/√2. P is scale invariant, but the scalar defect and curvature-response comparisons must use the matching Einstein constant.

The X→∞ formula already gives a useful benchmark for the proposed θ repair. In the Step-7 convention v₋=δu₁−δu₃, put k(x)=(x/(1+x))² and f=f₋. The outgoing antisymmetric perturbation

v₋(x)=c f(x),   k(x)θ(x)=−(c/2)∫ₓ^∞f(s)²ds

satisfies the torsion-free relation and tends to zero in both components. Its raw transverse P quadratic action vanishes because (v₋/f)′=0; remote smooth truncations can make the quadratic cutoff cost tend to zero. Thus θ cannot restore positive definiteness in every outgoing direction. At an entrance ρ, this mode selects the null relation

2k(ρ)Θ + [V/f(ρ)]∫ᵨ^∞f(s)²ds=0.

This is not a zero-cost whole cell: extension through a smooth bolt is missing, and the relative calibration still carries its entrance transgression. It sharpens the next question to the cost of reaching this null relation from the bolt, together with coercivity transverse to it.

On the inner side, distinguish admissible bolt data from a variational response. Smooth bolt regularity alone does not specify a Lagrangian costate plane; that plane must come from a stationary extremal or the Hessian of a minimized core action. Propagating −Φ, or linearizing around a witness whose stationarity remains unresolved, does not establish that identification. A finite-interface core minimization with bolt area allowed to vary, or an explicit lower action for those core traces, would make the matching consequential. It could yield the needed lower estimate—or reveal a bolt-compatible direction that improves the construction. This is where the new exterior understanding should now be invested.

The agreement between the trace-derived λ, the fitted tail, and the truncation law is a substantive reason to deepen the core–exterior reduction. There is an inherited variational identity that can make its target sharper. I54 §8 rescales to

δJ₆[2φg]=4∫φ(Δ₊+6)(s+24).

Thus a smooth complete finite-J₆ critical limit, whose admissible variations include compactly supported radial conformal changes, must have s≡−24: test the scalar equation with cutoffs and use s+24∈L². Consequently J₆=P exactly at such a limit. This does not force the metric to be Einstein and does not exclude a nonzero λ. It supplies a geometric stationarity condition beyond small coefficient gradients and suggests eliminating or solving the conformal direction in the reduced problem. The LM improvement is real, but finite-basis stationarity is not yet stationarity among all diagonal metrics; the inherited nonattainment theorem also still excludes a fully critical smooth cell with a fixed open CH collar.

The next important distinction is between the exact quadratic terminal cost and a nonlinear transparent boundary condition. Because δ²/I vanishes on the Einstein mass line, smallness of the boundary trace does not automatically give a multiplicative nonlinear error bound relative to this cost. On the null line the quadratic term is zero, while higher-order cost may remain. Either integrate that null direction into a local nonlinear family of Einstein exterior metrics and measure displacement transverse to that family, or retain its nonlinear residual explicitly in the terminal response. The symmetric and scalar trace sectors likewise cannot be left uncharged when the core endpoint is freed.

This makes the finite-interface problem a strong next investment: determine the actual core–exterior critical balance, with the scalar constraint and a controlled nonlinear terminal response. It can establish a meaningful limiting geometry and provide the correct boundary momenta for a lower certificate. Merely optimizing the core against the rank-one quadratic penalty could instead exploit directions absent from the model, even while reproducing the present witnesses very accurately.

The scalar issue can potentially become a reduction rather than another growing set of numerical variables. In four dimensions, the inherited conformal identities give, along the normalized Yamabe deformation ∂τg=−2(s+24)g,

 dJ₆/dτ=−4∫(|∇s|²+6(s+24)²),   dP/dτ=−∫|∇s|²,

whenever the boundary terms vanish. Thus this particular scalar-normalizing deformation decreases the intended full functional—and P as well—unlike arbitrary minimization of the scalar residual. For complete CH-asymptotic profiles with uniformly negative scalar curvature, investigate convergence to s=−24 with sufficient decay to justify these identities. That would supply a conformal-selection lemma for the candidate class and remove the scalar direction from the infinite-ended variational problem.
